title: Citta the teacher
hook: a householder who taught monks and debated wanderers (SN 41)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jivaka, the baby found on a rubbish heap who grew up to care for the Buddha's body. Your line was the healer. Whose health did you look after? Today, a householder the monks went to for answers. Day seven hundred seventy.

A group of elder monks has come back from the alms round, and they're stuck. Sitting together in a pavilion after their meal, they're discussing a question about the mind, and they don't agree. Some answer one way, some another. A householder named Citta, in the next village on some business of his own, hears about it. He walks over, pays his respects, and asks: is it true you were discussing this? It is, they say. A householder of the town of Macchikasanda. Not a monk. Today, his answer, and what the elders said to it.
screen: `THE ELDERS DISAGREE.` → `A HOUSEHOLDER HEARS.` → `IS IT TRUE?`

segments.voice: First, the question. The fetter, and the things that can fetter, like the eye and what it sees: are they one thing under two names, or different things? Some elders say one thing, some another. Second, the picture. Citta answers with two animals. A black ox and a white ox are tied together by a single yoke. Is the black ox the white ox's fetter? Is the white ox the black one's? Neither, he says. The yoke is the fetter. In the same way, the eye isn't what binds forms, and forms aren't what binds the eye. The desire and lust that arise between them, that's the fetter. Third, the praise. The elders tell him it's his good fortune: he has the eye of wisdom that reaches into the Buddha's deep words. Fourth, the record. That talk opens a whole chapter of the Samyutta given to Citta. In it he questions monks, answers them, and talks with teachers of other schools. And in the Anguttara's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha names Citta of Macchikasanda as the foremost of his lay men who teach the Dhamma. That's where this week has led. It began with the women of the first sangha, founders, mothers and queens. Then Anathapindika, who gave a grove and kept giving when he was poor. Jivaka, who gave medicine. And now Citta, who gave answers. A householder teaches.
screen: `ARE THE FETTERS THE THINGS THEY BIND?` · `TWO OXEN, ONE YOKE.` · `THE EYE OF WISDOM.` · `FOREMOST OF LAY TEACHERS.` · then, large: `A HOUSEHOLDER TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach from where you are. Settle, and breathe. No robe or title needed. Bring to mind one thing your own life has taught you well: how to calm a crying baby, how to fix a dripping tap, how to get through a long shift, how to apologize. Then think of one person who could use it. Find the plainest picture for it, like Citta's two oxen and one yoke. Offer it only if it would really help. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Gahapati, householder. What Citta of Macchikasanda was, answering the elders with two oxen and a yoke, and named foremost of the lay teachers. Today's word.
Your line: a householder teaches. Today, share one plain thing you know, simply, with someone it would help. Day seven hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities today, lay men and women also teach the Dhamma, lead study groups and meditation sessions, and give talks at temples and centers, alongside monks and nuns.

fork.setup: you're Citta, a householder. you hear that the elder monks nearby are split on a question about the mind. what do you do?
options: stay out of it; it's monks' business.
go to them, ask about it, and offer an answer.
wait for the Buddha to settle it.
fork.reveal: he goes, asks whether it's true, and answers with two oxen and a yoke. the elders tell him he has the eye of wisdom.

original.note: Pali gahapati: householder, the head of a household; the texts call him Citta the householder.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the Buddha's time, only monks taught.
what it means: a householder answers the elder monks with a plain picture, two oxen and one yoke.
what a scholar hears: a whole chapter of the Samyutta, SN 41, collects Citta's talks, and the Anguttara names him foremost among lay men who teach the Dhamma.
recall: foremost among nuns in psychic power

notes: SN 41.1 paraphrased. Confirm: the elders at the Ambataka grove, Macchikasanda, discussing after the meal in the pavilion; Citta arriving at Migapathaka on business; the question whether fetter and things that fetter are different in meaning and phrasing or one; the black ox and white ox yoked by a single yoke or harness; the elders' praise ('a gain for you ... the eye of wisdom that ranges over the deep word of the Buddha').
Etadagga (AN 1.14): Citta of Macchikasanda as foremost among male lay disciples who are speakers on the Dhamma; confirm.
Talks with teachers of other schools (e.g. SN 41.8, 41.9) are mentioned only in passing and without any judgment of those schools.
Week-end look-back covers days 764–770 (the women, then the first lay followers).
Editor: removed 'a family and land' (not in SN 41.1); restated the elders' question closer to the sutta (fetter vs. things that can fetter: one or different).

Auditor (serious): in SN 41.1 Citta hears of the elders' discussion and goes to them himself; the elders did not 'put the question to him', and the text says they answered differently, not that they were 'stuck'. Hook, hook screen heads and fork rewritten to match.
